name: Autism Spectrum Test
tagline: Explore whether you share traits common on the autism spectrum.
intro: This screener looks at four areas linked to autistic traits in adults: social interaction, communication, sensory sensitivity and routines or focused interests. Answer based on how you usually are, not on how you would like to be. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis, but it can help you decide whether a professional assessment is worth exploring.
seoTitle: Autism Spectrum Test – Free adult autism screener
seoDescription: Do you recognise autistic traits in yourself? Take this 5-minute adult screener on social, communication, sensory and routine traits and get a report.

social.name: Social interaction
social.short: How natural or effortful social situations and understanding others feel to you.
social.low: Your answers suggest that social situations mostly feel natural to you. You seem to pick up on what others think and feel, and socialising does not drain you more than average. Everyone has awkward moments, so occasional discomfort is normal. Keep using the social strengths you have, and remember that needing some time alone now and then is perfectly healthy.
social.mid: Your answers suggest that some parts of social life take extra effort for you. You may enjoy people but find groups tiring, or understand others well one-to-one while unwritten rules in larger settings feel less clear. Notice which situations cost you the most energy and plan recovery time afterwards. Choosing smaller gatherings or activities with a shared focus can make socialising more enjoyable.
social.high: Your answers suggest that social interaction often feels confusing, effortful or draining for you, and that you may adapt or mask a lot to fit in. These experiences are common among autistic adults, although they can have other causes too. If they affect your work, friendships or wellbeing, consider talking to a qualified professional experienced in adult autism assessment. Meanwhile, give yourself permission to recharge and seek out people who accept you as you are.

communication.name: Communication
communication.short: How you process and use language, tone, hints and non-verbal signals.
communication.low: Your answers suggest that you communicate with relative ease. You seem to pick up hints, tone and humour without much effort and adjust your style to different people. Misunderstandings still happen to everyone, but they do not seem to be a pattern for you. Your flexible communication style is a real strength at work and in relationships. If you ever feel misunderstood, simply asking a clarifying question usually resolves it quickly.
communication.mid: Your answers suggest a mixed picture. Some aspects of communication, such as vague instructions, fast group conversations or expressing feelings, may take more effort than others. It can help to ask for clarity directly and to tell people you prefer clear, concrete information. Writing things down before an important conversation can also make it feel easier and less tiring. Notice which settings work best for you and seek them out.
communication.high: Your answers suggest that you often process communication differently from those around you: you may take words literally, prefer directness or find tone and hints hard to read. This is a well-known pattern on the autism spectrum and is not a flaw, just a different style. If it causes frequent misunderstandings or stress, consider speaking with a qualified professional. Explaining your communication preferences to the people close to you can also prevent many conflicts.

sensory.name: Sensory sensitivity
sensory.short: How strongly you react to sounds, light, touch, smells and other sensory input.
sensory.low: Your answers suggest that everyday sensory input rarely bothers you. Noise, light, textures and crowds do not seem to overwhelm you more than most people. That makes busy environments easier to handle. Still, it is worth noticing whether you sometimes push past your limits without realising it, especially when you are tired or stressed. Regular quiet moments help keep it that way, even if you rarely feel overloaded.
sensory.mid: Your answers suggest that some sensory experiences bother you more than average. Certain sounds, textures or busy places may wear you down, especially on demanding days. Small adjustments can make a big difference: noise-reducing headphones, comfortable clothing, softer lighting or planned quiet breaks. Paying attention to your sensory needs is not fussiness, it is smart self-care. Keep track of which situations drain you most so you can plan around them.
sensory.high: Your answers suggest that you are highly sensitive to sensory input and that ordinary environments can quickly feel overwhelming. Strong sensory sensitivity is very common in autistic people, but it also occurs with anxiety, ADHD or high sensitivity in general. If it limits your daily life, consider discussing it with a qualified professional, such as a psychologist or occupational therapist. Protect yourself with tools like earplugs, sunglasses and regular quiet time to recover.

patterns.name: Routines and focused interests
patterns.short: How much you rely on routines, focus deeply on interests and notice details.
patterns.low: Your answers suggest that you are flexible and comfortable with change. You adapt easily when plans shift, enjoy variety and your interests come and go naturally. This flexibility helps in unpredictable situations. If you ever want to deepen a skill, a little more structure and focus can be a helpful complement to your adaptable style. Simple routines, such as a fixed time for important tasks, can support you without limiting your spontaneity.
patterns.mid: Your answers suggest that you appreciate some predictability and may have a few interests or habits you feel strongly about, while still coping with change reasonably well. Routines can be a real source of calm and productivity. When change is coming, try to prepare by gathering information in advance. Your eye for detail and focus can be a genuine strength in the right setting.
patterns.high: Your answers suggest a strong preference for routine and predictability, intense focused interests and a sharp eye for detail and patterns. These traits are typical of the autism spectrum and can be real strengths, for example in specialised work. If unexpected change causes you a lot of distress, consider talking to a qualified professional who understands autism. Building predictable routines and preparing for transitions can help you feel more in control.

summary: This screener shows how strongly you recognise traits that are common on the autism spectrum in four areas. Higher scores mean you recognise more of these traits in yourself. Many people score high on one area only, and the results are not a diagnosis: only a qualified professional can assess autism.
